extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and judges (practitioners of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and doctrinal criteria governing assignments, licenses, reissues, extensions, disclaimers, estoppel, and related title questions under U.S. patent law (case law and statutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption as to term in assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: The only presumption applicable to contracts for the sale of a patent interest is that the parties dealt for the existing term, unless a provision was inserted in the grant or assignment looking to a further interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the assignment instrument is silent as to future terms, reissues, or extensions, courts will normally construe it as transferring rights only for the then-existing patent term. An explicit clause is required to transfer future or extended interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment language covers future patents/extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Language conveying 'all the right, title, and interest' in an invention/patent is construed broadly to include patents already issued and all which 'might be issued thereafter' — including reissues, renewals, and extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad, all‑encompassing grant language (e.g., 'all right, title and interest... and all alterations and improvements... whenever issued') is interpreted to transfer future patents/renewals/extensions to the assignee. Courts will enforce the parties' apparent intent when such broad wording is present (Railroad Co. v. Trimble).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of inchoate rights vests legal title before issuance
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment executed before the patent issues (of the inchoate right) may operate to vest the assignee with the legal right to the monopoly when the patent later issues; the assignment of the whole interest before issue is effective to transfer the future legal title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the invention is complete and specification prepared, an assignment of the whole interest (even before issuance) will be treated as intended to operate upon the perfect legal title when obtained; courts reject formalistic requirements for a second transfer after issue (Gaylor v. Wilder, discussed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue applications to assignees — historical practice and statutory change (1870)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the statute of 1870 the Patent Office often granted reissues to assignees (even assignees of assignees) without the original patentee joining; the statute of 1870 (section 33) changed this by providing patents may be granted/reissued to assignees only where the assignment is first entered of record and the inventor makes the application and swears to the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the historical Patent Office practice (pre-1870) versus the post-1870 statutory rule: after 1870 assignments must be recorded and the inventor must be the applicant and swear to the specification for patents/reissues issued to assignees. A later act limited application of §33 to patents issued after July 8, 1870. Case law prior to 1870 may reflect the older practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office practice re: reissue by partial or territorial assignee (Commissioner discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office (and its commissioner) historically refused reissue applications made by an assignee who did not hold the whole interest in the patent (e.g., only an exclusive territorial interest), and courts have sometimes declined to definitively rule on that practice but signaled it may be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An assignee who holds less than the whole interest (e.g., all rights except certain states) may face refusal of a reissue application by the commissioner; the Supreme Court in Commissioner v. Whitely declined to decide definitively but suggested the commissioner's refusal could be correct. Practitioners should ensure the applicant holds the requisite interest or join necessary parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment versus license distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment transfers an interest in the patent (the monopoly) — either the whole or an undivided part, possibly exclusive as to territory, and may include the right to grant to others; a license is a grant or permission to practise the invention or use the patented thing that leaves legal title and the patentee's residual interest intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key practical consequences: assignments (if full for the territory) generally can be recorded and assignees may sue in their own name; licenses need not be recorded and licensees cannot normally sue for infringement in their own name. Determine whether the instrument transfers the monopoly (assignment) or merely permits use (license) by examining whether the grantee acquires a legal estate and the right to grant others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial exclusive grant that transfers full control is an assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instrument vests in the grantee the exclusive right, for the whole country or for a particular district, to make and use the patented thing and to grant that right to others, it is an assignment; any conveyance short of transferring the entire monopoly in the territory is a license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where the instrument does not literally use the words 'to grant to others,' courts will construe an instrument as an assignment for a territory when its fair construction excludes the patentee from control and transfers the entire interest within the specified territory (Perry v. Corning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reservations by patentee indicate license (not assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee reserves rights (for example, the right to send machines of his own manufacture into the territory), the instrument is more likely a license rather than an assignment of the entire territorial interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A retained right by the patentee to continue certain activities in the territory suggests the grantor did not transfer the whole interest; such instruments have been held to be licenses even if exclusive rights were granted to the grantee in other respects (Hussey v. Whitely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignability and apportionability of licenses depends on instrument terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere license (personal permission) is generally not assignable unless the instrument shows an intent to make it assignable; the use of the word 'assigns' in a license does not automatically make it assignable, and some licenses represent an entirety incapable of lawful apportionment among multiple assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret each license in light of its whole tenor and the parties' intent. Courts have held certain licenses (e.g., granting a single 'right' to employ a specified number of persons) cannot be subdivided and assigned in severalty (Brooks v. Byam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of recitals/covenants in license — estoppel of licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'naked' license or permission to work under a patent, without recitals or covenants amounting to admissions, does not estop the licensee from denying the patent's validity or denying that he used the patented thing. But recitals or covenants in the instrument that admit use or validity may estop the licensee from asserting invalidity in subsequent proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully review license language: admissions that the process used is the patented process or recitals as to novelty/utility/sufficiency of the specification can operate as estoppels in covenant or infringement suits. If the patentee joins issue rather than pleading estoppel, the deed may be admissible evidence but not conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment and restitution when patent is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee who has paid an annuity and derived the benefit of the license generally cannot recover the payments on the ground of patent invalidity (payment was for the benefit received). However, where there has been no enjoyment by the licensee and no covenant/admission, invalidity may be set up as failure of consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the licensee has actually benefited from the license payments, courts often refuse restitution even if the patent proves invalid; conversely, if payments were made but the licensee had no enjoyment or the contract fails, invalidity can support a failure-of-consideration defense (Hayne v. Maltby and subsequent explanations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee's right to contest validity when sued for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a licensee can contest the validity of the patent when sued for infringement depends on the license's terms: absent admissions or estoppel the licensee may challenge validity; if the license contains admissions or the licensee seeks to repudiate the license and assert invalidity, he forfeits benefits of the license and may still be estopped by contractual admissions unless deceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensee who stops paying or repudiates the license to claim the patent is invalid gives up the license's protections; courts will permit contesting validity where there are no estoppel-producing recitals, but admissions or covenants in the deed may bar such defenses unless fraud or deception is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture clauses — dual remedies and injunctive relief
rubrics_metrics.description: A clause making a license void on non-payment or breach of conditions gives the patentee a double remedy: he may either sue for the unpaid money or treat the license as forfeited and proceed to enjoin the licensee as an infringer. Breach of conditions (e.g., selling outside territory) works a forfeiture and permits injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees can elect remedies; the presence of a forfeiture clause should be considered strategically (sue for damages or rescind license and enjoin). Conditions limiting sales/territory can be enforced by injunction upon breach (Woodworth v. Weed; Wilson v. Sherman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of treating a license as forfeited — assertion of prior rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee elects to treat a license as forfeited and proceeds against the licensee as an infringer, the defendant may be remitted to any rights he had anterior to the license (e.g., a prior title or right existing before the license). It is, however, questionable how far this permits the defendant to avoid admissions in the license regarding validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a license is declared void and the patentee sues as for ordinary infringement, the defendant can assert prior subsisting rights he held before the license. Whether this allows avoidance of admissions about validity contained in the license is unclear and not fully settled by the cited decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers — who may file and effect on assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: When a disclaimer is filed under the relevant statutory sections, an assignee of the whole patent is the proper party to file it; if the patent had been assigned in part previously, the disclaimer will not operate to the benefit of an assignee (in suit) unless that assignee joined in the disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer executed under the seventh and ninth sections should be joined or filed by the assignee of the whole patent to protect assignee interests; partial assignees should join disclaimers to obtain their benefit in litigation (Wyeth v. Stone, cited).
